title: Chapter 106 — Ahab’s Leg
paragraphs: The hasty manner in which Captain Ahab had left the Samuel Enderby of London had not been without some small violence to his own person. He had landed with such energy upon a thwart of his boat that his ivory leg had received a half-splintering shock. And when, after gaining his own deck and his own pivot-hole there, he so vehemently wheeled round with an urgent command to the steersman — it was, as ever, something about his not steering firmly enough — then the already shaken ivory received such an additional twist and wrench that, though it still remained intact and to all appearances strong, Ahab did not consider it entirely trustworthy.

And indeed it seemed small wonder that, for all his pervading mad recklessness, Ahab did at times give careful attention to the condition of that dead bone upon which he partly stood. For it had not been very long before the Pequod's sailing from Nantucket that he had been found one night lying face-down upon the ground, unconscious — by some unknown and seemingly inexplicable accident, his ivory limb having been so violently displaced that it had stake-like pierced, and all but run through, his groin. Nor was it without extreme difficulty that the agonizing wound was entirely cured.

Nor, at the time, had it failed to enter his obsessive mind that all the anguish of that present suffering was but the direct consequence of a former woe. And he too plainly seemed to see that as the most poisonous reptile of the marsh perpetuates his kind as inevitably as the sweetest songbird of the grove, so, equally with every happiness, all miserable events naturally beget their like. Yes, more than equally, thought Ahab; since both the ancestry and posterity of Grief go further than the ancestry and posterity of Joy. For not to hint of this: that it is an inference from certain canonical teachings that while some natural pleasures here shall have no children born to them for the other world, but shall be followed by the joy-childlessness of all hell's despair; whereas some guilty mortal miseries shall still fertilely beget to themselves an eternally progressing offspring of griefs beyond the grave — not at all to hint of this, there still seems an inequality in the deeper analysis of the thing. For, thought Ahab, while even the highest earthly joys ever have a certain petty insignificance lurking in them, but at bottom all heartaches carry a mystic significance, and in some men an archangelic grandeur — so do their diligent tracings-out confirm the obvious conclusion. To trail the genealogies of these high mortal miseries carries us at last among the sourceless firstborn of the gods; so that, in the face of all the glad, hay-making suns and soft chiming harvest-moons, we must surrender to this: that the gods themselves are not forever glad. The indelible, sad birthmark in the brow of man is but the stamp of sorrow in the signers.

Unwittingly here a secret has been divulged which perhaps might more properly have been disclosed before. Along with many other particulars concerning Ahab, it had always remained a mystery to some why, for a certain period both before and after the sailing of the Pequod, he had hidden himself away with such grand-lama-like seclusion, and for that one interval sought speechless refuge, as it were, among the marble senate of the dead. Captain Peleg's rumored reason for this seemed by no means adequate, though indeed, as touching all Ahab's deeper nature, every revelation partook more of significant darkness than of explanatory light. But in the end it all came out — this one matter did, at least. That dreadful mishap was at the bottom of his temporary seclusion. And not only this, but to that ever-shrinking circle ashore who, for any reason, possessed the privilege of a less prohibited approach to him — to that timid circle the above-hinted accident, remaining as it did moodily unexplained by Ahab, invested itself with terrors not entirely unrelated to the land of spirits and of wails. So that, through their concern for him, they had all conspired, so far as they could, to hush up the knowledge of this thing from others. And hence it was that not till a considerable time had passed did it come to light upon the Pequod's decks.

But be all this as it may; let the unseen, ambiguous powers in the air, or the vindictive princes and potentates of fire, have to do or not with earthly Ahab — yet in this present matter of his leg, he took plain practical steps: he called the carpenter.

And when that functionary appeared before him, he ordered him without delay to set about making a new leg, and directed the mates to see him supplied with all the studs and joints of jaw-ivory — sperm whale — which had thus far been accumulated on the voyage, in order that a careful selection of the stoutest, clearest-grained stuff might be secured. This done, the carpenter received orders to have the leg completed that night, and to provide all the fittings for it, independent of those pertaining to the distrusted one in use. Moreover, the ship's forge was ordered to be hoisted out of its temporary idleness in the hold; and to speed the affair, the blacksmith was commanded to proceed at once to the forging of whatever iron parts might be needed.
